requirement: Smooth a numeric series with a trailing moving average, optionally padded with NaN to line up with the original timestamps.
skeleton: moving_average converting to float64, validating dimensionality and an inclusive window range, averaging sliding_window_view rows, and optionally prepending window-1 NaN.
caption: A trailing moving average in NumPy built on sliding_window_view. moving_average(values, window, *, pad=False) converts values to a float64 array and raises ValueError saying values must be 1-D for any other shape, and ValueError saying window must be between 1 and the length when window is outside that inclusive range. It takes sliding_window_view of the data with the window and averages each window along axis 1, giving len minus window plus 1 means. With pad True it prepends window minus 1 NaN values with np.full so the result has the input length and each mean sits at the end of its window. The fixture asserts that 1 to 6 with window 3 gives 2, 3, 4, 5, that padding yields length 6 with two leading NaN, that windows equal to the length and to 1 are valid, that windows 0 and 4 on three values raise ValueError between 1 and 3, and that 2-D input raises ValueError.

plan.intent: Smooth sensor readings for a chart
constraints: Each output is the mean of one full window
The unpadded length is len - window + 1

rationale.teaches: sliding_window_view gives a zero-copy window matrix; reduce along the window axis and handle edge windows and padding length exactly.
rationale.why: Reducing the wrong axis averages positions instead of windows, and off-by-one padding shifts every smoothed point relative to its timestamp.

ops.docstring: Trailing moving averages with NumPy sliding windows.

candidates.why_wrong: Means are taken across windows instead of within each window.
A window equal to the series length is rejected.
Padding adds one NaN too many and shifts every average right.
Leading slots are padded with zeros that look like real averages.
2-D input is windowed across both axes instead of rejected.
